lessons.title: Wants, needs, scarcity and choice

objectives: Distinguish wants from needs and economic goods from free goods.
Explain scarcity, choice and opportunity cost.
Read a simple production possibility curve.
reviewNotes: All prices, quantities and FCFA amounts are invented teaching figures, not real market data.

blocks.title: Wants, needs and scarcity
blocks.md: **Wants** are the things people would like to have; they are unlimited. **Needs** are things required to live, such as food, water, clothing and shelter. **Resources** (land, labour, capital, enterprise) are limited. This gap is called **scarcity**. Because of scarcity, people, firms and governments must make **choices**.

blocks.title: Opportunity cost
blocks.md: Every choice means giving something up. The **opportunity cost** is the **next best alternative** that is given up when a choice is made. A **scale of preference** lists wants in order of importance, so the item at the top is chosen first. **Economic goods** are scarce and have a price; **free goods** (such as air) are not scarce.

blocks.caption: A production possibility curve for cocoa and maize with points on, inside and beyond it (schematic).
blocks.alt: A curve bowed outwards from top-left to bottom-right with a point on the curve, a point inside it and a point outside it.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: Opportunity cost is **not** the price paid and **not** the total of all alternatives: it is the **one best alternative** forgone. Scarcity does not mean poverty: rich and poor countries both face scarcity. Wants for one person may be needs for another, so always say which meaning you use in an answer.

blocks.title: Production possibility curve
blocks.md: A **production possibility curve (PPC)** shows the largest combinations of two goods an economy can make when all resources are fully used. A point **on** the curve is efficient, a point **inside** shows unemployed resources, and a point **beyond** the curve cannot be reached now. Producing more of one good means producing less of the other.

blocks.title: Worked example — opportunity cost of a choice
blocks.statement: Ebot has 10 000 FCFA. He can buy shoes (10 000 FCFA), a set of textbooks (8 000 FCFA) or school fees contribution (6 000 FCFA). He ranks them in this order: shoes, textbooks, fees contribution. He buys the shoes. What is his opportunity cost?
steps: He cannot afford all three, so he must choose.
His top choice is the shoes, so he buys them.
The next best alternative is the set of textbooks, so that is the opportunity cost (not the fees contribution).

blocks.title: Worked example — cost in goods
blocks.statement: A farmer in Bali can use one plot to grow 600 kg of maize or 300 kg of groundnut (illustrative). What is the opportunity cost of 1 kg of groundnut in kg of maize?
steps: Growing groundnut gives up 600 kg of maize.
That sacrifice is spread over 300 kg of groundnut.
600 ÷ 300 = 2 kg of maize per kg of groundnut.

lessons.title: Factors of production and division of labour
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Economics — basic economic problem (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the four factors of production and their rewards.
Explain division of labour and specialisation, with advantages and disadvantages.
reviewNotes: All prices, quantities and FCFA amounts are invented teaching figures, not real market data.
The order and depth of topics are an editorial choice to be checked against the Cameroon GCE Board O Level Economics syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Four factors of production
blocks.md: **Land** means all natural resources (soil, forests, water, minerals, oil). **Labour** is human effort, physical or mental. **Capital** is man-made goods used to produce others (machines, buildings, tools); it is different from money. **Enterprise** is the work of the entrepreneur who organises production and takes risks. Their rewards are **rent, wages, interest and profit**.

blocks.title: Division of labour and specialisation
blocks.md: **Division of labour** splits the making of a product into separate tasks, each done by a different worker. **Specialisation** means a worker, firm, region or country concentrates on what it does best. Example: in a garment workshop one person cuts, another sews and a third irons. It works best when the market is large enough to buy all the extra output.

blocks.caption: The four factors of production, an example of each and the reward it earns.
blocks.alt: A table with three columns, factor, example and reward, and four rows for land, labour, capital and enterprise.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
blocks.md: **Advantages**: workers become faster and more skilled, less time is lost moving between jobs, machines can be used, output per worker rises and unit costs fall. **Disadvantages**: work is boring, workers lose wider skills, one stoppage can halt the whole line, and workers are hard to replace when demand for the product falls.

blocks.title: Be careful with the words
blocks.md: Do not write that capital is 'money': in economics capital is **real** goods such as machines. Land includes natural resources, not only farms. Labour is paid **wages** (not salaries only), and profit is the reward for **enterprise**, not for labour. Specialisation and division of labour are linked but not identical.

blocks.title: Worked example — output per worker
blocks.statement: A workshop in Limbe has 12 tailors, each making a complete shirt alone. Each tailor makes 8 shirts a week. After tasks are divided, the same 12 tailors make 480 shirts a week. Find output per worker before and after (illustrative).

blocks.title: Worked example — classify the factors
blocks.statement: A woman in Kumba uses her plot, a hired helper, a hand mill and her own planning to produce cassava flour. Name the factor each represents.
steps: The hired helper is labour and the hand mill is capital.
She plans and takes the risk, so she is the entrepreneur (enterprise).
